articles.title: A jury set to decide who owns the work of Henry Darger, Chicago’s most famous outsider artist
articles.text:
A jury set to decide who owns the work of Henry Darger, Chicago’s most famous outsider artist - WBEZ Chicago
Henry Darger spent four decades living alone in a one-room North Side apartment (seen here as a recreation at the Intuit Art Museum), creating art and writings that are now estimated to be worth millions. The fight over who legally owns his work is set to play out in a federal courtroom, beginning in March 2027.
Lisa and Nick Albertson
Art
History
Arts & Culture
A jury set to decide who owns the work of Henry Darger, Chicago’s most famous outsider artist
A federal judge set a March 8 trial date for the case filed in 2022. Would-be heirs say they are the rightful owners of Darger’s works, trademarks and copyrights.
By
Stefano Esposito
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
A federal jury is soon expected to decide who legally owns the artwork and writings of Henry Darger, more than 50 years after the death of the North Side hermit. The work is estimated to be worth millions of dollars.
This week, U.S District Court Judge Thomas Durkin set a March 8, 2027 date for a jury trial, expected to last about a week.
“A case filed in 2022 deserves to get a trial date,” Durkin told the attorneys in the case Thursday.
Darger died April 13, 1973, leaving behind a one-room Lincoln Park apartment at 851 W. Webster Ave., crammed with broken furniture, old record players and other debris he’d plucked from garbage cans. But beneath the trash, lay an extraordinary trove of his life’s work: hundreds of watercolors, collage paintings and, in a trunk, a 15,000-page typed fantasy novel titled “In the Realms of the Unreal.”
Outsider artist Henry Darger’s former home, located at 851 W. Webster Ave.
Pat Nabong/Sun-Times
Darger never married. He had no children. He was an unknown artist in his lifetime. His landlords, Nathan and Kiyoko Lerner, took possession of Darger’s works after, in failing health, he moved out of the apartment and into a Catholic nursing home. Kiyoko Lerner, who now lives in Japan, has testified that Darger told her husband that he no longer wanted his art and that Nathan Lerner could have it.
That artwork is now worth millions. Darger is considered among the world’s greatest “outsider” or self-taught artists. Over several decades, Kiyoko Lerner (Nathan Lerner died in 1997) has sold, reproduced, donated, exhibited and licensed countless Darger works, including selling at least 22 pieces to the American Folk Art Museum in New York for a total of $1 million in 2000.
The Art Institute of Chicago, the Intuit Art Museum and the Museum of Modern Art in New York all own Darger pieces.
But Darger left no written will. And so in 2022, a group of people claiming to be distant Darger relatives filed suit in federal court, arguing, among other things, that they are the rightful owners of Darger’s works, trademarks and numerous copyrights.
One of the potential heirs, Kristin Klein, spoke to the Sun-Times shortly after the federal suit was filed in 2022. Klein was living in Connecticut at the time.
Works by Chicago artist Henry Darger, courtesy of Robert A. Roth, displayed at Intuit: The Center for Intuitive and Outsider Art in 2008. The mixed media creations are titled “Cat Headed Blengian,” left, and “Spangled Winged Tuskorhorian Blengin.” The reclusive writer-artist died in 1973 at age 81.
Charles Rex Arbogast/AP
“I kind of think that us being relatives, yeah, we deserve part of his estate,” Klein said in 2022. “Just because we weren’t around when he was alive doesn’t mean that people who weren’t related to him deserve to have his entire estate. It should have gone to family to begin with.”
Darger’s state of mind in his declining years will likely come into play during the trial. Alan Jay Mandel, an attorney for the would-be heirs, told Judge Durkin Thursday that he is considering having a mental-health expert testify at trial.
In pre-trial court filings, attorneys for the potential heirs point to, among other things, Darger’s death certificate, which lists “senility” as a cause of death. Durkin has said in a written ruling in the case that the senility diagnosis is relevant, but that “the certificate does not establish as a matter of law that Darger lacked the capacity to make a gift.”
The trial will certainly attract attention from across the artworld, particularly among representatives of art galleries and museums that have Darger pieces in their collections.
One person who won’t be there is Ron Slattery, who died earlier this year.
Originally from Chicago, Slattery was a vintage photography collector. He and his wife, Fawn Slattery, were the ones who originally tracked down a potential Darger relative in 2019 to alert her to her possible claim to Darger’s art and writings.
The Slatterys told the Sun-Times back in 2022 that they had never met the Lerners but felt the former landlords shouldn’t profit from Darger’s talent. The Lerners’ supporters have said that Darger would likely have remained unknown without the Lerners’ help in preserving and putting his artwork and writings out into the world.

Pat Nabong/Sun-Times

City inspects funeral home where 55 decaying bodies were found amid calls for its demolition
South Chicago Chapel, 2939 E. 95th St., was shut down after the gruesome discovery on Aug. 6.
By
Mohammad Samra
Updated
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
How the funeral industry fails Illinois' bereaved.
As the Chicago Department of Buildings conducted an inspection Friday morning at the South Side funeral home where 55 decomposing bodies were found in August, activists and a family impacted by the discovery called for the building’s demolition.
“This is a house of horrors we’re standing next to,” said Lisette Guillen, a crisis responder with Case Files Chicago. “The way families feel — the way most of Chicago and the surrounding areas feel — is it probably should be knocked down.”
The inspection comes over two months after authorities ordered the building shut down after the decaying bodies were found by police acting on a tip.
Guillen cited a number of hazards both for impacted families and the immediate surrounding community to justify demolishing the building.
“There’s children that are here. There’s pets that walk on the grass and take things back inside the home,” Guillen said. “We don’t know what the area around may have been exposed to.”
Over six months after her mother Shawnese Shannon died from advanced cancer, Marshawna Campbell and her family are still left with questions and uncertainty.
When Campbell learned that the man who had picked up her mother’s body from hospice had been accused of mishandling human remains, she and her sister opened their mother’s urn and began to question everything after finding cremated remains that looked like chunks of white substance.
“All of our questions are still unanswered,” Campbell told reporters outside the funeral home Friday morning. “We couldn’t even celebrate my mama being gone for six months because we don’t know if it’s her in the urn.”
A lack of information from police has left Campbell frustrated, and her voice cracked as she questioned how Clark and Johanna Morgan, the owners of the funeral home, allowed the conditions.
“What if it was you in our shoes?” Campbell said. “All y’all did was burn her skin and break her bones. I could’ve done that myself.”
Inspectors were inside the building for over 30 minutes and came out around 10:45 a.m. without speaking, and the city’s Department of Buildings, which dispatched the inspectors, did not respond to a request for comment about what they saw or whether there was any communication with the Morgans.
Also at the site of the inspection was Ald. Peter Chico (10th) and an SUV believed to be registered to Clark Morgan, though it could not be confirmed whether he or his wife were there.
Chico also did not respond to a request for comment about the inspection.
The Department of Buildings said in a statement that inspectors from the department’s electrical, new construction, plumbing and demolition bureaus were at Friday’s inspection, and that they will present findings in court on Oct. 29 during a hearing.
“The Department of Buildings recognizes the deep pain the families are experiencing, and our thoughts remain with them as this process moves forward. Today’s inspection was conducted pursuant to a court order requiring the Department to conduct a comprehensive inspection of the building,” the department said.

articles.title: CPS high school graduation and college enrollment rates rise, but many students still struggle to finish
articles.text:
CPS high school graduation and college enrollment rates rise, but many students still struggle to finish - WBEZ Chicago
A higher share of Chicago Public Schools students are graduating from high school and enrolling in college. But CPS graduates complete college at a much lower rate than their peers nationally.
Pat Nabong/Sun-Times file
Education
Chicago School Board
Education
CPS high school graduation and college enrollment rates rise, but many students still struggle to finish
The district’s graduation rate has been steadily growing since the early 2000s when fewer than half of students were earning a diploma in four years.
By
Emmanuel Camarillo
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Chicago Public Schools students are increasingly earning college credits while still in high school and are graduating and enrolling in college at higher rates than in the past, but many still struggle to finish college and earn a degree.
Those are among the findings of a report released Friday by the To&Through Project and the UChicago Consortium on School Research, coupled with district data released earlier this week.
The report found that 56% of CPS students who graduated in the class of 2019 and immediately enrolled in a four-year college got their degree or a workforce certificate within six years, while 32% of those who immediately began at a two-year institution earned a degree or certificate within the same time period. Those percentages have barely budged for four years.
Overall, only 48% of 2019 CPS graduates who immediately enrolled in college earned a degree or certificate within six years, the report found — far below the 64% national rate.
At the same time, CPS students are graduating and enrolling in college at or near all-time high rates. CPS’ graduation rate rose to 82.6% for the class of 2025, and the graduation rate rose again for the class of 2026 to 83.4%, district officials said this week.
Meanwhile, 67% of the class of 2025 immediately enrolled in college, up from 58% a decade ago and above the national average, according to the report.
The data indicates that while more high schoolers are reaching the next level of their education, many still need additional resources and support once they get there.
But Dominique McKoy, executive director of the To&Through Project, added that it also shows how far graduation rates have grown in recent decades.
“We got to remember that within living memory this was a district in the city that had a high school graduation rate of 50%,” he said. “We had some community areas in the city of Chicago with high school graduation rates of 25%.”
The report also found persistent racial and gender disparities within college completion rates.
Among 2019 CPS graduates, young men were much less likely to graduate with a college degree in six years than young women — a pattern that held true across every racial and ethnic group, according to the report. The disparity was especially stark for young Black and Latino men, with fewer than one-third of whom graduating with a bachelor’s degree within six years.
Young Latina women, Asian and Pacific Islanders and white students in the class of 2019 completed a degree or certificate at higher rates, the report found.
Mckoy said that the data provides “probably some of the strongest evidence around the necessity around initiatives” such as CPS’ Black Student Success Plan, which aims to reduce academic disparities among Black students.
The report notes that students who started college in 2019 and those that graduated high school in 2025 went through major events that affected their schooling, such as the COVID-19 pandemic and the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign last year.
Still, overall college completion rates among CPS students have slowly increased over time.
The percentage of CPS graduates who enrolled in a four-year college and completed a degree of any kind within six years increased from around 53% to just under 56% from the class of 2010 to 2019. And that increase was even higher for those who enrolled in two-year colleges.
The district’s graduation rate has risen steadily over the past two decades. In 2000, less than half of CPS students graduated within four years, district data show. CPS reached its all-time high graduation rate in 2023, when nearly 85% of students got their diploma on time, according to the To&Through and UChicago report.
These students are earning college and workforce credentials during their high school years at a higher rate, too. More than 57% of CPS graduates in the class of 2026 earned college credits and career certificates, 10 percentage points higher than four years ago, according to district data released this week.
That includes technical certifications in skilled trades, credit for Advanced Placement courses and the seal of biliteracy, an award that recognizes students who demonstrate proficiency in English and another language, which can qualify for college credit.

articles.title: DOJ allowed to join lawsuit against Evanston reparations program for Black residents
articles.text:
DOJ allowed to join lawsuit against Evanston reparations program for Black residents - WBEZ Chicago
Pro-reparations yard signs sit outside homes in Evanston, just over a week after the Evanston City Council approved a first-in-the-nation reparations plan to make amends for historical wrongs against Black residents, Tuesday afternoon, March 30, 2021.
Ashlee Rezin Garcia / Sun-Times
Race, Class & Communities
Politics
Housing
DOJ allowed to join lawsuit against Evanston reparations program for Black residents
Evanston’s reparations program has faced years of legal challenges. It may now face its largest challenge yet after a district judge approved the DOJ’s motion to join a lawsuit seeking its dismantlement last week.
By
Zoe Singer
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
The Department of Justice is officially allowed to join a lawsuit against Evanston’s historic yet highly contested reparations program after a judge approved the agency’s motion last week, according to court records.
District Judge John F. Kness approved the DOJ’s motion to join a 2024 class-action legal challenge from Judicial Watch, a conservative nonprofit, against the City of Evanston’s reparations program, which launched in 2021 with the stated goal of remediating past racial housing discrimination of Black residents between 1919 and 1969.
Joining six residents who are not Black but say their relatives lived in Evanston during the 50-year reparation qualification period, the DOJ claims the program violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and the Fair Housing Act.
“Evanston has chosen to distribute substantial benefits to persons solely because of their race or the race of their ancestors,” the federal government’s motion states. “The Program does not provide any opportunities for compensation for residents of other races who may have lived in the area where black residents were segregated and suffered adverse housing consequences as a result.”
The first U.S. city to fund a local reparations program, Evanston officially approved its program in 2021.
Nearly five years later, the Justice Department announced in June its intention to join the Flinn, et al. v. City of Evanston lawsuit and now has the necessary approval to move forward with its plan.
“This is an effort to intimidate,” former Evanston mayor Daniel Biss told WBEZ in July after the DOJ announced its plan to join the lawsuit. “This is an effort by the Trump administration to tell anyone who’s interested, ‘back off, we’re going to come for you.’”
Evanston’s first reparations policies offered a maximum of $25,000 in housing grants to Black people who lived in the city or had ancestors who lived in the city during the 50-year period of racially discriminatory housing policies. In 2023, Evanston amended its policy to offer eligible applicants unrestricted cash payments, rather than requiring the $25,000 to go toward housing subsidies.
The DOJ’s brief emphasized that Evanston no longer requires beneficiaries “to provide any account of how they use the funds.”
The Evanston accepted reparation applications for 45 days in 2021 and has not accepted any applications since November 5 of that year, according to the DOJ. In a 2024 motion to dismiss the case, the City of Evanston stated it “does not have any current plans to reopen applications.”
Evanston paid 141 applicants who qualified as an “Ancestor” and has begun paying 454 others who qualified as “Direct Descendants,” totaling more than $5 million worth of reparation, according to the DOJ.
In its lawsuit, the DOJ acknowledges instances in which race can be used when “remediating specific, identified instances of past discrimination that violated the Constitution or a statute.” But the Department details that Evanston’s program is too general and does not identify a specific scope of past discrimination the city intends to correct.
“The City’s racially discriminatory program is not narrowly tailored to remedy specific identified instances of past discrimination,” the brief states. “They contain virtually no information about what the alleged discriminatory acts or policies were, during what years the discriminatory acts occurred, the policies that were in effect, or the scope of the injury caused by these acts or policies.”
Biss, who ended his second mayoral term on Sunday and is running to represent Illinois’ 9th congressional district in Congress, has been at the forefront of the reparations program since its founding. During his July interview, he rejected the claim that Evanston’s program is not specific in its eligibility requirements or intended goals.
“The city dug deep in our history. We worked with scholars to understand what we’ve done. We documented real harm that not only happened in the past but is being felt right now by residents of Evanston,” the then-Evanston-mayor told WBEZ.
Evanston motioned for the case to be thrown out in July 2024, stating that the six complainants had not proven they were “ready” and eligible to apply for the grants during the time the program was accepting applications, notwithstanding their racial identities.

articles.title: Salt Shed owners eye amphitheater expansion across from popular West Town venue
articles.text:
Salt Shed owners eye amphitheater expansion across from popular West Town venue - WBEZ Chicago
The Salt Shed is looking to expand by building an outdoor amphitheater at an empty lot next door, 1459 N. Magnolia Ave., along the North Branch of the Chicago River.
Mark Black/For the Sun-Times
Real Estate & Development
Money
Arts & Culture
Salt Shed owners eye amphitheater expansion across from popular West Town venue
The expansion would include an outdoor plaza and potential pedestrian bridge spanning the North Branch of the Chicago River.
By
Abby Miller
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
The Salt Shed could soon see a sister venue across the street that would include an amphitheater, bar and outdoor plaza.
The expansion plans were outlined in a zoning application filed with the City Council on Oct. 14 by a limited liability company tied to the Salt Shed.
The plans note that Blue Star Properties and 16” on Center, the hospitality collective whose portfolio includes Empty Bottle, SPACE, Thalia Hall and the Salt Shed, don’t own the land where the expansion is proposed. But if a sale goes through, the plot at 1401-59 N. Magnolia Ave. would expand the companies’ entertainment holdings and the industrial-to-entertainment transformation happening along the North Branch of the Chicago River.
The companies didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Plans for Salt Shed’s expansion first emerged in October 2025, when Crain’s Chicago Business reported the venue’s owners were targeting the empty parcels for an outdoor music venue.
The site span 516,316 square feet and hugs the east side of the Chicago River. The lots are sometimes used for parking during shows and other events at the Salt Shed.
The empty lot at 1459 N. Magnolia Ave. across the street from Salt Shed is where the venue wants to expand, with an outdoor amphitheater along the North Branch of the Chicago River in Chicago on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026.
Mark Black/For the Sun-Times
Site plans show a parking lot along West Le Moyne Street, with roughly 100 spaces for attendees and artists. Next to the lot would be offices and a building with artist dressing rooms, and the rest of the site, near West Blackhawk Street, would have an amphitheater and seating. There would also be a VIP seating section close to the stage, flanked by a general admission standing area and tiered seating behind it. In the center, behind VIP seating, is a bar.
West Blackhawk Street — which separates the Salt Shed and the prospective amphitheater — would be transformed into a landscaped public plaza connecting the two venues. Plans also show a pedestrian bridge on a portion of the street that would connect the venues. West Blackhawk Street is already closed during shows for security and entry lines.
The expansion would be a huge boon for the Salt Shed’s owners. The former Morton Salt factory venue is selling out most shows, the Sun-Times and WBEZ previously reported, and leaning into an on-site music village concept with a record store, guitar shop and food trucks. Earlier this year, tattoo parlor Deluxe Tattoo opened an outpost at the Salt Shed, offering tattoos inspired by artists performing at the venue.
The Salt Shed has a capacity of roughly 5,500 people for outdoor shows and 3,600 for indoor shows. The site plan doesn’t specify the capacity of the new amphitheater, though Crain’s Chicago Business previously reported it could be up to 15,000.

articles.title: The Rundown: A traffic nightmare on the Kennedy Expressway

The Rundown: A traffic nightmare on the Kennedy Expressway - WBEZ Chicago
The Kennedy Expressway.
Manuel Martinez/WBEZ
The Rundown: A traffic nightmare on the Kennedy Expressway
Plus, how to register to vote. Here’s what you need to know today.
By
Bianca Cseke
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share

Good afternoon! It’s Friday, and my cats approve of the humans who helped after a Chicago rescue’s window was broken. Here’s what you need to know today.
1. 3 years later, the traffic nightmare on the Kennedy Expressway lives on
If you’re among the legions of Kennedy Expressway commuters who had to put up with gridlock over the past few years and swear you’ve never been in traffic this bad — you’re right.
My colleagues Dan Mihalopoulos and Alden Loury analyzed 22 years of drive-time data and found delays on the expressway between Downtown and O’Hare Airport were the worst in more than two decades during the rehabilitation project that began in March 2023 and ended last October.
Most of the longest Kennedy commutes on record occurred during the three-year project, as the state of Illinois spent more than $170 million working on the 7.5-mile stretch between Downtown and the Edens Expressway junction.
Despite Gov. JB Pritzker’s promise of “faster commutes” when he declared mission accomplished on the Kennedy project a year ago, the expressway has continued to post historically bad travel times this year. That’s as the separate Foster Avenue bridge reconstruction project over the Kennedy on the Northwest Side has lagged far behind schedule, according to documents obtained by WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times.
June 2025 saw the worst backups ever on the outbound Kennedy, with drivers facing an average commute time of 74 minutes to get from Downtown to O’Hare between 2 and 3 p.m. on weekdays during that month. Average outbound travel times exceeded 65 minutes for each hour between noon and 7 p.m. on weekdays that month. [ WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times]
2. It’s not too late to register to vote. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot by Nov. 3
While you can no longer register to vote online through the state’s board of elections website (registration closes 16 days before Election Day), you have a few in-person options.
When applying for or renewing your driver’s license or state ID card at a DMV, you will be asked if you want to register to vote. If you answer yes, you will be required to attest, under penalty of perjury, that you meet the qualifications to register to vote and provide your electronic signature.
Multiple local government offices register voters in-person, including the county clerk’s office, board of election commissioners office, city and village offices, township offices and military recruitment offices.
Illinois allows same-day registration at early voting sites and on Election Day. You must bring two forms of ID or proof of residency. The state allows for several types of ID and proof of residency, including a passport, driver’s license, student ID, pay stub, lease, medical bill or mortgage. At least one ID must list your current address. For example, your state driver’s license with an old address plus a copy of a ComEd bill with your current address will work. [ Chicago Sun-Times]
3. Chicago passengers could see a fuel surcharge on taxi fares
As my colleague Cindy Hernandez reports, the surcharge is implemented when both AAA’s current average and month-ago average price for regular gasoline in the Chicago area reaches at least $5 per gallon.
Taxi drivers can charge $1 if the fare is $20 or less; $2 for fares between $20.01 and $40; and $3 for fares $40.01 or more. The surcharge applies to the fare before taxes, tolls and additional fees are added. A notice must be posted inside the cab. [ Chicago Sun-Times]
In other transportation news, CTA Brown, Green, Orange and Pink line trains won’t be able to access Loop elevated tracks during repair work this weekend. Shuttle buses will be available. [ Chicago Sun-Times]
4. After a year of unusual weather in Chicago, should you brace for winter?
Chicago can expect a milder winter due to a potentially “historically strong” El Niño, according to the National Weather Service’s winter outlook report released last week. As Amy Yee writes for the Chicago Sun-Times, that means a 50% to 60% chance of above-normal temperatures this winter. But the weather service said even a mild winter will likely have stretches of cold weather and snowstorms.
The National Weather Service is a U.S. government agency under the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration with nearly 150 weather forecast offices and centers. Forecasters use computers to analyze observations from surface stations, weather balloon readings, radar and satellite data. A seven-day forecast is accurate about 80% of the time — but a forecast of 10 days or longer is accurate only about half the time, the NOAA said.
Across the northern U.S., the weather service also expects warmer than normal temperatures from December to February. In addition, it forecasts wetter than average conditions across the southern U.S. and along the East Coast. [ Chicago Sun-Times]
5. A jury is set to decide who owns the work of Henry Darger, Chicago’s most famous outsider artist
More than 50 years after the death of the North Side hermit, Darger’s art and writing is estimated to be worth millions of dollars, my colleague Stefano Esposito reports. This week, U.S District Court Judge Thomas Durkin set a March 8, 2027, date for a jury trial, expected to last about a week.
Darger died April 13, 1973, leaving behind a one-room Lincoln Park apartment at 851 W. Webster Ave., crammed with broken furniture, old record players and other debris he’d plucked from garbage cans. But beneath the trash lay an extraordinary trove of his life’s work: hundreds of watercolors, collage paintings and, in a trunk, a 15,000-page typed fantasy novel titled “I
